name: Imperial Red
lede: Imperial red is a strong, slightly bluish red whose name has pointed at an old court color, a pigment lake and the modern screen swatch.

sections.title: Three meanings
sections.body:
Paterson defines imperial red as a deep bluish red, among colour names that borrow the word imperial for majesty, like imperial yellow, originally a Chinese porcelain color reserved for the court [1]. In pigment lists, Heaton (1928) records imperial red as a then-current synonym for an eosin lake [2]. Eosin is a bright pink-red dye, struck onto a base to make paint [2].

Pastoureau mentions an older imperial red as well: Charlemagne's traditional mantle, which late medieval artists replaced with blue [3]. These are three different uses, and the sources do not link them. The swatch here is ISCC-NBS strong red, from the 1955 system, nine units from the nearest block center [4]. Neighbors include [[red]], [[scarlet]], [[crimson]], [[carmine]] and [[vermilion]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Only 4 of 23,781 archive paintings contain this color, rarer than 77 percent of named colors [5]. That is too few for painter or period patterns. As photographed, a bright red in aged paintings has usually shifted, so the match counts a screen look-alike, not a dye.
